Engineering physics on track

Hover or tap a highlighted section of the circuit. Select it to open the diagram. Zones illustrate what a car could do there, based on the map geometry. Replay speed stays uniform.

Illustrative values. The reference map and lap timing do not supply forces, braking points, or local speeds.

0.0 s

Monza 2024 sector comparison

Compare sector splits for two lap selections. A negative gap means a shorter time in the Verstappen column.

How to read the sector gaps
  • Sector gap is the Verstappen column minus the Norris column for that split. A negative value means a shorter time in the Verstappen column.
  • Cumulative gap adds the sector gaps up to that point. For example, −0.300 s in Sector 1 and +0.100 s in Sector 2 leave a −0.200 s gap after Sector 2.
  • Finish gap uses the two reported lap durations directly. If a sector is missing, the cumulative gap is unavailable from that point, but the finish gap can still be calculated when both lap durations are present.

A sector gap shows where time changed. Speed, brake and throttle traces would be needed to investigate how it happened.

Times and gaps in seconds
SplitVerstappenNorrisGapCumulative gap

What the comparison means

Fastest recorded race lap by either driver of the selected constructor at this circuit in that car’s season. Average speed is the source’s lap-average speed, not maximum or instantaneous speed. Different seasons, drivers, tyres, fuel, weather and traffic prevent a controlled car-only comparison.

What the animation means

Cars move at uniform distance per second around a community reference layout, using the recorded lap duration when available. No corner-speed, braking, throttle or tyre telemetry is inferred. This simplified 800 kg car runs on a flat road with zero vertical acceleration. Arrows show force direction and vary in length, with a minimum visible size. Positions are schematic. The top-view diagram shows lateral acceleration separately.

Orange · acceleration along the carGreen · acceleration across the car

Equations and assumptions

Speed depends on the reference line’s curvature and a lateral acceleration limit of 22 m/s². Acceleration is limited to 5 m/s² and braking to 12 m/s² across the full loop.

Lateral acceleration is v²κ, where κ is signed curvature. Drag, downforce and drag power are ½ρv²CᴅA, ½ρv²|Cʟ|A and drag × speed. The model uses ρ = 1.225 kg/m³, CᴅA = 1.5 m² and |Cʟ|A = 4.5 m².

The arrows show the two acceleration components. The speed model uses separate limits and omits combined tyre grip, banking, elevation, gears and wind. Aero values are calculated alongside motion and do not feed back into the speed model. This is a simulated lap with the Qvist concept car shown with a top-down projection.

Vehicle dynamics at this point

Play or scrub the lap to compare tyre demand, axle loads and power at the same instant.

Combined tyre grip

Circle radius = μN. The dot combines forward or braking force with lateral force. Demand beyond the circle exceeds this illustrative grip budget. The replay speed is calculated independently.

Longitudinal transfer is −Fₓ,tyre h/L. A negative value means load shifts rearward. Lateral transfer is |Fᵧ|h/t across the whole car.

Corner geometry and motion

Local radius
Signed yaw rate
Signed lateral force

Fᵧ = mv²κ and yaw rate = vκ. Curvature κ comes from the reference line. Positive lateral values point right in the top-view diagram.

Energy and power

Kinetic energy
Power absorbed at braking tyres
Power lost to air drag
Rate of change of kinetic energy

Eₖ = ½mv². The tyre and drag forces do work at the rate (Fₓ,tyre − D)v. Braking power shows the tyre contribution during braking, before any brake or energy-recovery split.

Vehicle assumptions and model limits

Illustrative 800 kg car with a 0.32 m centre-of-gravity height, 3.60 m wheelbase, 1.65 m track width and constant μ = 1.65. At zero longitudinal transfer, 46% of weight and downforce acts on the front axle. Drag acts at the centre of gravity.

The diagnostic uses a lumped tyre-force circle. Individual tyre loads, load sensitivity, aero balance changes, suspension and roll stiffness, differential and brake bias, thermal effects, and banking are outside this model.

Mechanics of a lap

Work–energy theorem

From replay start to the current position, ΔK = Wtyres − Edrag. Gravity and the normal force do no work along the level path in this model. A full lap can end at the same kinetic energy even though the engine has supplied work against air drag.

Change in kinetic energy
Energy lost to drag
Net longitudinal tyre work
ΔK
−Edrag
Wtyres

The energy bars share a zero line. Left is negative and right is positive. The scale follows the largest magnitude at the selected position.

Work at the vehicle’s centre of mass. Net tyre work includes both positive drive work and negative braking work. The model does not track the total energy of the engine, brakes and tyres.

Banking and the direction of friction

For a separate idealised curve, try setting the bank angle and moving the speed through v₀ = √(rg tan θ). Below v₀, friction points up the bank. Above it, friction points down the bank.

  • Green · Normal
  • Blue · Weight
  • Amber · Friction

Resolve the forces

On an 80 m radius with μ = 0.8 and no aero, N = m(g cos θ + v² sin θ/r). Taking down the bank as positive, f = m(v² cos θ/r − g sin θ). No slip in this model requires |f| ≤ μN. Above that limit, the arrow shows the direction of the friction that would be required to hold the prescribed path. The diagram uses fixed-length normal and weight arrows and varies the friction arrow for visibility.

Drifting, sideslip and steering

The body angle and the direction of travel can differ. β is the angle from vehicle heading to centre-of-mass velocity. Tyre slip angle in this diagram is wheel heading minus local axle velocity direction.

Kinematic example at 20 m/s and +0.30 rad/s yaw rate. It illustrates angles. Calculating a sustained drift also requires tyre forces, drive torque and yaw dynamics.

Stanford study on drifting and sideslip

Rotation, rolling and friction

Translation follows ΣF = ma. Yaw, the rotation about the vertical axis, follows Στz = Izαz. Front and rear tyre forces act at different distances from the centre of mass, so equal net lateral force can still produce different yaw torques.

Pure rolling gives v = ωR at a wheel. For an ideal rigid wheel on a stationary surface, the instantaneous point of contact is at rest. Real tyres deform, can develop slip, and dissipate energy.

Work through the yaw moment

An 800 kg car with a 2,000 N lateral force at the front and 3,000 N at the rear has 5,000 N net lateral force. If the forces act 1.9 m ahead of and 1.7 m behind the centre of mass, respectively, the yaw moment is 3,800 − 5,100 = −1,300 N·m with the front moment taken positive.

EXPERIMENT / PIPELINE

From movement to meaning.

  1. Collect real gesturesMultiple people, sessions, backgrounds. Idle is a required class.
  2. Split by participantSeparate train, validation and test people before tuning.
  3. Compare architecturesMean-pooling MLP → LSTM → temporal Transformer.
  4. Tune on validation onlyOptuna search with pruning and early stopping.
  5. Evaluate & deployMacro-F1, confusion matrix, CPU latency and checkpoint size.
